newsitem.title: FRANCE: French crops can bear new dry spell - analysts.
newsitem.headline: French crops can bear new dry spell - analysts.

text.p: Dry warm weather returned to France this week but crop experts and weather forecasters said there was no cause for alarm yet as substantial rain earlier in May had brought plants enough moisture to get through the next two to three weeks.
"May rainfall was above the average for the month and the plants did absorb most of it. They have reserves for at least 15 days," a Meteo France forecaster told Reuters.
"There is no reason to panic because it has not rained for a few days," crop analyst Andree Defois of Strategie Grains said, adding crops should be comfortable for at least three weeks.

Meteo France said the weekend should be dry and sunny in northern France while scattered showers and thunderstorms were in store for the south. Forecasters did not expect any significant break in the weather pattern next week.
"There will still be some showers in the south but the north should remain dry," one said.

Rainfall for May was 70 mm for the north, 110 mm in the southwest and 80 mm in the west, well above averages for the month. But precipitation in the southeast was only 17 mm in May against an average of 57 mm, Meteo France said.

Forecasters and analysts said substantial rain in May helped crops recover from nearly four months of drought in key grain and beet production basins of northern France but were not sufficient to help replenish depleted ground water tables.
The rain, however, came too late to help grain crops in the south, where sharp yield losses are forecast.
Defois predicted wheat and barley yields may fall by 15-20 percent in the south. The region is not a major grain producer, having less than 10 percent of the total acreage sown in France.

National grain office ONIC predicted earlier this month a 20-30 percent fall in yields in the south. Durum wheat suffered most from the drought with some analysts predicting yield losses of up to 50 percent.

May rain also helped the sugarbeet crop make good progress and plant development as of May 20 was in line with an average year, planters said this week. Warm and wet conditions did increase pest pressure across France but counter-measures have proved successful, they said.
Defois said that at this stage there was no reason to change the prediction she made last month of slightly lower wheat and barley yields for 1997.
"A wheat yield of nearly seven tonnes is satisfactory even if is slightly below last year's level," she said.
She said France's wheat and grain crop would need to benefit from end of cycle weather conditions similar to last year to reach the records seen in 1996.
Last year's record grain harvest of 62 million tonnes came after rain in May and June helped crops recover from a prolonged dry spell in the spring.
Strategie Grains predicted last month a 1997 wheat yield of 6.98 tonnes, below the 7.27 tonnes reached last year and a barley yield of 5.97 tonnes per hectare against 6.19 tonnes in 1996.

Assuming higher wheat and barley sowings, France would harvest a soft wheat crop of 34.41 million tonnes and barley crop of 9.62 million tonnes, after the 1996 wheat crop of 34.69 million and barley crop of 9.46 million tonnes.
